papers.title: GEO: Generative Engine Optimization
papers.authors: Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, Tanmay Rajpurohit, Ashwin Kalyan, Karthik Narasimhan, Ameet Deshpande
papers.key_findings: Coined GEO and defined the field's canonical visibility metrics. (1) Word-count impression: Imp_wc(c_i,r) = sum of lengths of sentences citing source c_i divided by total response length. (2) Position-adjusted word count: Imp_pwc(c_i,r) = sum over citing sentences of |s|*e^(-pos(s)/|S|), normalized by total response word count, so earlier sentences carry exponentially more weight; word credit is split equally when a sentence cites multiple sources. (3) Subjective impression: GPT-3.5 rates seven G-Eval-style dimensions (relevance, influence on response, uniqueness, subjective position, subjective content volume, click likelihood, diversity), normalized to the same mean/variance as position-adjusted word count. Content tweaks (adding quotations +41%, statistics +33%, fluency +29% on position-adjusted word count) boost source visibility; keyword stuffing does not. Effects replicated on live Perplexity.ai (200-query subset: quotations +22%/+32%).
papers.methodology_notes: Simulated engine: top-5 Google results fed to gpt-3.5-turbo at temperature 0.7; 5 responses sampled per query 'to reduce statistical deviations'; experiments repeated over 5 random seeds with averages reported and standard deviations in appendix; no formal significance tests. Metric formulas extracted from the full HTML version (arxiv.org/html/2311.09735v3).
papers.relevance: The metric toolbox to adapt: replace 'source' with 'brand' and Imp_pwc becomes a position-weighted brand share-of-answer usable per prompt-language-engine cell. The 5-samples-per-query practice is the closest precedent for the study's 5 repetitions per cell, and the paper's own caveat that efficacy 'varies across domains' motivates splitting skincare vs fashion. Its LLM-judge subjective metric is optional garnish; the objective word-count metrics are cheap and reproducible from captured answers.

papers.title: GEO-bench (official dataset release for the GEO paper)
papers.authors: GEO-Optim (Aggarwal, Murahari et al.)
papers.key_findings: 10,000 queries (8K/1K/1K train/val/test) drawn from nine sources (MS MARCO, Natural Questions, ORCAS-I, AllSouls, LIMA, Davinci-Debate, Perplexity Discover, ELI5, GPT-4-generated), each paired with cleaned text of the top-5 Google results, tagged across ~25 domains and 7 query categorizations including intent.
papers.methodology_notes: Dataset card confirms per-query structure (query + 5 cleaned sources) and the tag taxonomy; supports both objective and subjective impression scoring.
papers.relevance: Its query taxonomy (intent, difficulty, domain tags) is a template for documenting the 10 purchase-intent prompts. Note the gap the study fills: GEO-bench is English-only and not commerce-focused; there is no code-mixed or India-geolocated slice, which is precisely the study's contribution.

papers.title: C-SEO Bench: Does Conversational SEO Work?
papers.authors: Haritz Puerto, Martin Gubri, Tommaso Green, Seong Joon Oh, Sangdoo Yun
papers.key_findings: First multi-domain, multi-actor benchmark of conversational SEO. Visibility is quantified as the change in a document's citation rank within the engine's answer after applying a C-SEO method. Two tasks (web QA: news/debates/general web; product recommendation: retail products, video games, books). Headline results: most published C-SEO methods are ineffective or hurt ranking; traditional SEO transfers better; and when multiple actors adopt the same optimization, gains collapse toward zero-sum (diminishing returns with adoption rate).
papers.methodology_notes: 16,360 items across six domains (count per the GEO-Bench 2026 paper's reuse of the data); code at github.com/parameterlab/c-seo-bench, data at huggingface.co/datasets/parameterlab/c-seo-bench with results organized {partition}/{method}/{model}. Introduces an evaluation protocol that varies the fraction of adopting actors.
papers.relevance: Validates product recommendation as a first-class GEO task and supplies a rank-in-answer metric: for each brand, record its rank order within the recommendation list, not just presence. Its multi-actor framing also suggests reporting brand-level results relative to competitors in the same answer, which is how the EN-vs-Hinglish deltas should be expressed (rank shifts, not absolute mentions).

papers.title: Ranking Manipulation for Conversational Search Engines
papers.authors: Samuel Pfrommer, Yatong Bai, Tanmay Gautam, Somayeh Sojoudi (UC Berkeley)
papers.key_findings: Formalizes conversational search ranking as an adversarial ordering problem over retrieved product websites and introduces a dataset of real consumer product sites. A tree-of-attacks prompt-injection technique reliably promotes low-ranked products, and the attacks transfer to production Perplexity.ai. Demonstrates that the ordering of products inside an LLM answer is a measurable, manipulable quantity with direct financial stakes.
papers.methodology_notes: Real-world consumer product website dataset; rank of the target product in the generated recommendation list is the outcome variable; code at github.com/spfrommer/cse-ranking-manipulation. arXiv record: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03589.
papers.relevance: Gives the study its dependent-variable framing for fashion/skincare prompts: treat each answer as a ranked brand list and measure rank movement across language arms. Also a reason to capture and archive the cited source pages at run time, since answer rankings are sensitive to what the retrieval layer surfaced that day.

papers.title: Don't Measure Once: Measuring Visibility in AI Search (GEO)
papers.authors: Julius Schulte, Malte Bleeker, Philipp Kaufmann (University of St. Gallen; Aurora Intelligence)
papers.key_findings: Single-shot visibility measurements are statistically unreliable. Across ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, and Perplexity over 45 days: day-over-day cited-source Jaccard was only 0.34-0.42 (roughly 65% turnover), and even simultaneous identical reruns overlapped only 0.32-0.43 Jaccard, proving most instability is stochastic generation, not the web changing. Brand mentions are more stable than citations (Jaccard 0.45-0.59). Convergence analysis recommends 7-8 runs per prompt per day and 21-28 day rolling windows before trusting per-brand detection rates or trends.
papers.methodology_notes: 8 prompts per campaign across 4 verticals (telecom, real estate, sporting goods, consumer electronics); brand detection via campaign lexicons of 32-51 brands with substring matching; metrics: Jaccard, Rank-Biased Overlap (p=0.9), Gini coefficient for citation concentration; bootstrap subsampling (2,000 iterations), 95% CIs. Full numbers from arxiv.org/html/2604.07585v1.
papers.relevance: The methodological backbone for the study's null baseline. The right test is: EN-vs-Hinglish overlap (Jaccard/RBO on brands and on cited domains) compared against within-language rerun overlap from the 5 repetitions; a language effect exists only if cross-language overlap is significantly below rerun overlap. Also a sober warning: 5 reps per cell is below their 7-8 run recommendation, so per-brand detection rates should be reported with intervals, not as point facts.

papers.title: Quantifying Uncertainty in AI Visibility: A Statistical Framework for Generative Search Measurement
papers.authors: Ronald Sielinski (IQRush)
papers.key_findings: Treats citation share, citation count, and citation prevalence as random variables and builds response-level bootstrap 95% CIs. Empirically (Perplexity, SearchGPT, Gemini; three shopping-adjacent topics; ~200 queries/topic/platform over 9 days plus 10-minute-interval sampling): repeated-run domain Jaccard medians of 0.29-0.31 (Gemini), 0.33-0.40 (SearchGPT), ~0.50 (Perplexity); citation distributions follow a power law; a motivating example shows a 9.5% vs 6.0% citation-share gap dissolving under overlapping CIs. Sample-size guidance for a 0.05-wide citation-share CI: ~40-50 queries (Gemini), ~90-100 (Perplexity), 150+ (SearchGPT, which also shows non-stationarity within samples).
papers.methodology_notes: Bootstrap resampling of whole responses with replacement (preserves within-response dependency); SHA-256 checksums of cited pages confirm variance comes from engine behavior, not source churn; industry-affiliated single author, disclosed methodology.
papers.relevance: Prescribes the exact statistical treatment for a 5-rep design: bootstrap at the response level, report CIs on brand-mention share, and refuse to headline differences whose intervals overlap. Its sample-size tables imply the 10-prompt study can credibly support coarse claims (mention/no-mention, large rank shifts, answer-language classification) but not fine-grained citation-share differences; write the limitations section accordingly.

papers.title: Who Owns the AI Recommendation? A Multi-Industry Empirical Map of Brand Category Ownership Across Large Language Models
papers.authors: Dmitrij Żatuchin (Estonian Entrepreneurship University of Applied Sciences; Rankfor.AI)
papers.key_findings: Maps brand-recommendation behavior with 250 brand-free category queries x 3 models (GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Perplexity sonar-pro) x 5 repetitions (3,750 calls). Defines reusable metrics: Category Ownership Index (brand mention frequency / total iterations, with dominance thresholds), Recommendation Share (mean COI per industry), Competitive Vacuum Index (1 - max COI), and Displacement Score (asymmetric substitution when a rival is absent). Findings: brand concentration is moderate (mean Gini 0.28, CI [0.16, 0.41]), only 8% of queries lack a dominant brand, and the three models agree on the top brand in just 41.6% of queries.
papers.methodology_notes: English-only queries; API access rather than web-UI capture; 5 repetitions per query-model cell is the same repetition count as the planned study; no geographic conditioning.
papers.relevance: The closest existing design to the planned study (category queries x 3 engines x 5 reps) and the source of directly liftable metrics: COI per brand per language arm, and cross-model agreement rate as a headline statistic. Its 41.6% cross-model agreement figure predicts engine will matter at least as much as language. Explicitly English-only with no geography, so an India-geolocated EN/Hinglish replication is a genuine, citable gap.

papers.title: Generative Engine Optimization: How to Dominate AI Search
papers.authors: Mahe Chen, Xiaoxuan Wang, Kaiwen Chen, Nick Koudas
papers.key_findings: Roughly 1,000 consumer ranking prompts across 10 verticals run on Perplexity (sonar-pro, search on), Claude 3.5 Sonnet with web search, Gemini 2.5 Flash with grounding, and gpt-4o-search-preview, benchmarked against Google. The only prior GEO work with a cross-language arm: base queries translated into Chinese, Japanese, German, French, Spanish, then cited-domain sets compared via Jaccard overlap. Languages shift citations more than paraphrases do (7 paraphrase templates produced 0.3-0.7 base-variant overlap; language switches produced far lower overlap, with GPT effectively switching site ecosystems by language while Claude stayed English-heavy). AI engines show overwhelming earned-media bias: for example 92.1% earned sources in US consumer electronics vs Google's 51.7%, with social sources near zero.
papers.methodology_notes: Jaccard on unique cited domains per query, averaged to vertical level; source-type coding into Brand/Earned/Social; regional (US/Canada) splits; no repetition-count or CI reporting found in the extracted sections. Full design details from arxiv.org/html/2509.08919v1.
papers.relevance: Direct precedent and directional prediction for the EN-vs-Hinglish comparison: prompt language demonstrably changes WHICH domains get cited and whether citations tilt toward target-language sites, with the effect size differing per engine. Reuse their per-engine cross-language Jaccard analysis and their Brand/Earned/Social source coding for the citation arm of the study. Crucially, they tested clean translations into major languages; romanized code-mixed Hinglish is untested territory, and their engine-specific asymmetries (GPT most language-sensitive) are hypotheses the study can check.

papers.title: GEO-Bench: Benchmarking Ranking Manipulation in Generative Engine Optimization
papers.authors: Ojas Nimase, Zhe Chen, Gengpei Qi, Yue Zhao (USC); Xiyang Hu (ASU)
papers.key_findings: Unifies evaluation of eight ranking-manipulation algorithms and ten white-hat strategies across five datasets (including C-SEO Bench's 16,360 items). Standardizes rank-movement metrics: Normalized Rank Gain (NRG), Success@alpha (target reaches top-alpha fraction of the ranking), Promote@alpha (promotion into top-alpha from outside), plus stealth metrics (Keyword Violation Rate, Perplexity Ratio). Finds black-box content rewriting matches gradient-based attacks on promotion with better fluency; no attack wins on promotion, stealth, and fluency simultaneously. Distinct from Aggarwal et al.'s GEO-bench despite the name.
papers.methodology_notes: Single target model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), which limits external validity to production engines; metrics are cleanly specified and portable.
papers.relevance: Supplies formalized rank-shift metrics the study can adopt without inventing anything: report NRG and Success@3 (brand appears in top-3 recommendations) per brand between EN and Hinglish arms. Also useful for terminology hygiene: cite it to disambiguate 'GEO-bench' (Aggarwal 2024 dataset) from 'GEO-Bench' (this 2026 manipulation benchmark) so reviewers do not conflate them.

lenses.lens_summary:
The GEO literature began as a content-optimization problem and has matured into a measurement science, and the measurement half is what the EN-vs-Hinglish study should lean on. Aggarwal et al. (KDD 2024) established the canonical visibility metrics: word-count impression share, position-adjusted word count with exponential position decay (Imp_pwc = sum over citing sentences of |s|*e^(-pos(s)/|S|), normalized by response length), and an LLM-judged subjective impression across seven dimensions. Everything since either refines the outcome variable (C-SEO Bench and the Berkeley ranking-manipulation paper move it to rank-in-answer for product recommendations; the 2026 USC GEO-Bench formalizes rank movement as Normalized Rank Gain and Success@alpha) or interrogates its reliability. All these metrics are computable from captured answer text plus citation lists, so the study can adopt them wholesale: brand-level mention share, position-weighted share, rank within the recommendation list, and Jaccard/RBO overlap of cited domains.

The single most important methodological development for this study is the 2026 variance literature. St. Gallen's "Don't Measure Once" showed that identical prompts rerun simultaneously overlap only 32-43% on cited sources (brands are steadier at 45-59%), that day-over-day source turnover is roughly 65%, and that per-brand detection rates stabilize only around 7-8 runs per prompt; Sielinski's bootstrap framework independently found repeated-run citation Jaccard medians of 0.29-0.50 across Gemini, SearchGPT, and Perplexity and showed apparent citation-share gaps dissolving under overlapping confidence intervals. This is exactly why the planned design's rerun-variance-as-null-baseline is the correct and defensible move: a language effect should be claimed only where EN-vs-Hinglish overlap falls detectably below same-language rerun overlap, and with 5 repetitions per cell the study should report bootstrap or Wilson intervals and confine headline claims to coarse outcomes (brand present/absent, top-3 membership, answer-language classification) rather than fine-grained share differences.

On the specific question of prompt language, the literature offers one direct precedent and one clear gap. Chen, Wang, Chen and Koudas (2025) is the only prior GEO work that translated queries across languages and measured citation shifts: they found language moves cited-domain sets more than paraphrasing does, with strongly engine-specific behavior (GPT switches site ecosystems by language, Claude stays English-heavy, Perplexity tilts toward target-language sites), and a systematic earned-media bias in all AI engines (up to 92% third-party sources vs Google's balanced mix). Żatuchin (2026) ran the nearest design twin — 250 category queries x 3 engines x 5 reps — and found the three engines agree on the top recommended brand in only 41.6% of queries, but tested English only. Nothing in this literature tests romanized code-mixed Hinglish, purchase-intent prompts, or India geolocation; the study therefore fills a real gap while being able to borrow every metric, the cross-language Jaccard analysis, the multi-run null baseline, and the rank-shift statistics from named prior work rather than inventing methodology.

papers.title: Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings
papers.authors: Berk Atil, Sarp Aykent, Alexa Chittams, Lisheng Fu, Rebecca J. Passonneau, et al. (incl. Breck Baldwin)
papers.key_findings: Five LLMs run with fully deterministic settings (temperature 0, fixed seed) still produce different outputs across runs. Accuracy varied up to 15% across naturally occurring repeated runs, with best-to-worst output gaps up to 70%, and no model delivered repeatable accuracy on all tasks. Introduces TARr@N (total agreement rate on raw output) and TARa@N (agreement on parsed answers); raw-output agreement is frequently far below 100%. Attributes instability partly to batched inference on shared serving infrastructure, meaning it will persist in production APIs.
papers.methodology_notes: 5 LLMs x 8 tasks, 10 repetitions per condition, zero-shot and few-shot; agreement measured with TARr@N and TARa@N over the 10 runs.
papers.relevance: Establishes that rerun variance exists even under the most deterministic settings available, so variance in ChatGPT/Gemini web UIs (no temperature control, default sampling) is guaranteed to be nonzero and must be measured, not assumed away. Justifies the study's core design decision to treat rerun variance as the null baseline against which any EN-vs-Hinglish difference is tested. Its 10-rep protocol is a useful anchor: 5 reps is half that, defensible for effect detection but not for precise per-prompt stability estimation.

papers.title: Paraphrase Brittleness in Production Retrieval-Augmented Commercial Recommendation: Reproducibility Below the Rerun-Stability Baseline
papers.authors: Will Jack, Noah Lehman, Keller Maloney, Sarah Xu (Unusual.ai)
papers.key_findings: Formalizes exactly the null-baseline logic this study needs: first measure how much recommendation sets churn on identical reruns, then ask whether a prompt manipulation exceeds that churn. Same-prompt, same-day, within-cell Jaccard overlap of recommended-brand sets was only 0.50-0.61, i.e. roughly half the brand set changes between identical runs. Cosmetic paraphrases dropped Jaccard to 0.288 (95% CI 0.215-0.361) and constraint-adding paraphrases to 0.135 (CI 0.098-0.175), 21-48 points below the rerun baseline. Reasoning-effort level had negligible effect on stability (bounded within -0.015 to +0.005).
papers.methodology_notes: Rerun baseline: 50 commercial prompts x 4 model cells (gpt-5.4-mini, claude-sonnet-4-6, each at low/high reasoning) x N=30 identical same-day reruns = 6,000 runs. Paraphrase arm: ~20 base prompts x ~5 variants across 5 axes x 3 cells x N=20 repeats (~6,000 runs). Brands extracted via dual-judge consensus (claude-haiku-4-5 + gpt-5-mini); Jaccard similarity on recommendation sets; bootstrap CIs.
papers.relevance: The single most directly transferable design. It supplies a concrete, citable expectation for the null: identical buying prompts rerun the same day overlap at Jaccard ~0.5-0.6 on brand sets. An EN/Hinglish pair is a strong cross-lingual paraphrase, so the study should expect language-pair Jaccard well below the rerun baseline if language matters, and it should compute within-language rerun Jaccard from its 5 reps as the comparison floor. Notably, one of its paraphrase axes was region/language bindings, making the Hinglish arm a natural extension. Also cautions that 5 reps yields noisier Jaccard estimates than their N=20-30, so aggregate across the 10 prompts rather than reporting per-prompt stability.

papers.title: Who Owns the AI Recommendation? A Multi-Industry Empirical Map of Brand Category Ownership Across Large Language Models
papers.authors: Dmitrij Żatuchin
papers.key_findings: 3,750 responses across 250 brand-free category queries, 5 industries, 3 models (GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Perplexity sonar-pro), each query repeated 5 times under a 'dice roll' stability protocol. Brand concentration was moderate rather than winner-takes-all (mean Gini 0.28, 95% CI 0.16-0.41). Cross-model agreement on the top-recommended brand occurred in only 41.6% of queries (64.4% mean pairwise agreement), i.e. which brand 'wins' depends heavily on the engine. Proposes Category Ownership Index, Displacement Score, and Competitive Vacuum Index as repetition-aware metrics.
papers.methodology_notes: 5 repetitions per query-model cell, temperature 0.3, identical system prompts; 250 queries x 3 models x 5 reps = 3,750 calls; brand mention frequency aggregated over the 5 reps.
papers.relevance: Direct precedent for exactly 5 repetitions per cell in a brand-recommendation audit across the same trio of engine families (OpenAI, Gemini, Perplexity Sonar) — citable justification for the study's rep count. Its mention-frequency-over-5-reps aggregation (a brand 'owns' a query only if it recurs across reps) is the right unit of analysis for the EN/Hinglish comparison. The 41.6% cross-model top-brand agreement also predicts that engine will be a larger source of variance than language, so the study should model engine and language effects separately rather than pooling.

papers.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.authors: Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, Sharan Narang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Denny Zhou
papers.key_findings: The canonical demonstration that sampled LLM outputs to one prompt disagree substantially with each other, and that aggregating over multiple samples (majority vote over sampled reasoning paths) is far more reliable than any single run: +17.9% on GSM8K, +11.0% on SVAMP, +12.2% on AQuA over greedy single-run decoding.
papers.methodology_notes: Samples multiple (typically 5-40) reasoning paths per question at nonzero temperature and marginalizes by taking the most frequent final answer; evaluated on arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks across PaLM/GPT-class models.
papers.relevance: The peer-reviewed academic anchor for two claims in the study's methods section: (1) a single run of a generative model is a sample, not 'the answer', so single-run brand comparisons are methodologically invalid; (2) aggregation across repetitions (e.g. a brand counts as recommended for a cell if it appears in a majority of the 5 reps) is the established remedy. Its finding that most of the aggregation gain arrives within the first handful of samples supports 5 reps as a reasonable cost-accuracy point.

papers.title: Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks
papers.authors: Lovish Madaan et al. (Meta / UCL)
papers.key_findings: Systematically measures variance components (seed variance across training initializations, monotonicity during training, bootstrapped 95% CIs) across standard LLM benchmarks and a large set of models. Shows variance differs widely by benchmark, that some benchmarks have low signal-to-noise, and that performance differences smaller than the measured variance band are not meaningful.
papers.methodology_notes: Empirical variance estimates over many open and from-scratch-pretrained models; reports per-benchmark variance magnitudes with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals; proposes variance-reduction techniques for choice tasks.
papers.relevance: Supplies the statistical framing the study needs to be publicly defensible: report an uncertainty band from the 5 reps (bootstrap over reps and prompts) and only claim an EN-vs-Hinglish effect when the between-language gap exceeds that band. Useful citation for reviewers asking why the study reports CIs on share-of-voice rather than point estimates from single runs.

papers.title: Towards Reproducible LLM Evaluation: Quantifying Uncertainty in LLM Benchmark Scores
papers.authors: Robert E. Blackwell, Jon Barry, Anthony G. Cohn
papers.key_findings: Shows LLMs remain stochastic even at temperature 0 with fixed seeds, that most published evaluations skip uncertainty quantification for cost reasons, and proposes a simple, cost-effective method for estimating the uncertainty of a score from a modest number of repeated runs, with practical reporting guidance.
papers.methodology_notes: Repeated experimental runs on cardinal-direction reasoning benchmarks across multiple models; examines how repetition count affects score stability and confidence-interval width; explicitly addresses the budget-vs-precision tradeoff in choosing repetition counts.
papers.relevance: The best citation for the '5 reps per cell' budget decision: it legitimizes small-N repetition schemes provided uncertainty is estimated and reported rather than pretending determinism. For a 10-prompt x 2-language x 3-engine x 5-rep grid (300 runs), the study can follow this paper's approach of reporting per-cell score plus CI, and acknowledging that 5 reps bounds but does not eliminate estimation noise.

papers.title: The Non-Determinism of Small LLMs: Evidence of Low Answer Consistency in Repetition Trials of Standard Multiple-Choice Benchmarks
papers.authors: Claudio Pinhanez, Paulo Cavalin, Cassia Sanctos, Marcelo Grave, Yago Primerano (IBM Research)
papers.key_findings: Using 10 repetition trials of identical multiple-choice questions, only 50-80% of questions get answered consistently by small models (2B-8B) even at low temperatures; medium models (50-80B) are substantially more consistent. Consistency varies strongly by model and temperature, and accuracy computed on the consistent subset correlates with, but differs from, overall accuracy.
papers.methodology_notes: 10 repeated trials per question on MMLU-Redux and MedQA; multiple temperatures; finetuned vs base variants; consistency = fraction of questions with identical answers across all trials.
papers.relevance: Even on constrained multiple-choice outputs, 20-50% of items flip across reruns, so free-form buying recommendations (a much larger output space) should be expected to churn at least that much, consistent with the ~0.5 Jaccard rerun baselines seen in recommendation studies. Also warns that consistency itself is model-dependent, supporting the study's per-engine (rather than pooled) variance baselines, and that reporting the share of prompt-cells with unanimous top-brand agreement across the 5 reps is a meaningful headline metric.

papers.title: AI Search Volatility: Why AI search results keep changing
papers.authors: Profound (research team)
papers.key_findings: Across ~80,000 prompts per platform re-asked one month apart (June-July 2025), the share of cited domains that were new (citation drift) was 59.3% for Google AI Overviews, 54.1% for ChatGPT, 53.4% for Copilot, and 40.5% for Perplexity. Over six months (Jan-Jul), drift grew roughly linearly to 70-90%. Headline: 40-60% of the domains cited for an identical question are different one month later; single-snapshot measurement charts noise.
papers.methodology_notes: ~80,000 prompts per platform, identical queries re-run at a one-month interval; drift = % of domains in later responses absent from earlier ones; per-engine breakdown; largest disclosed-methodology industry dataset found for citation churn.
papers.relevance: Sets expectations for the WHAT-sources-are-cited outcome: citations are the least stable layer, far noisier than brand mentions. Two consequences for the study: (1) run all 5 reps of every cell within a tight window (same day or two) so temporal drift does not masquerade as a language effect; (2) analyze citations at domain level, not URL level, and expect even the rerun baseline for citation overlap to be low. Perplexity's lower drift suggests engine-specific citation-stability baselines are needed.

papers.title: AI Mode Research: Sources, Volatility, & Differences between AIO and Organic Search
papers.authors: SE Ranking research team
papers.key_findings: 10,000 keywords run through Google AI Mode three times on the same day (June 20, 2025, US, logged-out): three-way exact-URL overlap across all runs was only 9.2% (Jaccard), domain-level 14.7%; pairwise overlap between any two runs was 18.5-19% for URLs and 26.6-27% for domains. AI Mode overlapped AI Overviews at only 10.7% (URLs) and top-10 organic at 14%.
papers.methodology_notes: 10,000-keyword set, 3 independent same-day parses, non-logged-in US sessions, Jaccard coefficient on cited sources; overlap also computed vs AI Overviews and organic top 10.
papers.relevance: The starkest same-day, identical-query churn number in the industry literature: ~91% of exact cited URLs differ across three same-day runs of a Gemini-family answer engine. Directly calibrates the study's Gemini citation analysis: with 5 reps, expect near-total URL-level churn within a single language, so the EN-vs-Hinglish citation comparison must use domain-level union sets across reps, and any 'Hinglish cites different sources' claim must beat this brutal within-language baseline.

papers.title: AI Brand Mention Volatility Study: 481 Sites Across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews
papers.authors: Advanced Web Ranking (author-attributed single-analyst study)
papers.key_findings: Tracking 481 websites across finance, education, health, and SaaS (20 keywords per niche) weekly for three weeks on ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews: only 49% of brands kept consistent visibility across all three weeks. Churn varied by vertical (finance 34.7% dropout vs health 10.7%) and by authority (78% of DA 70+ brands stayed stable; 64% of DA<50 sites dropped at least once). Engines showed different source profiles (ChatGPT skewed to publishers, 62% of mentions).
papers.methodology_notes: 481 sites, 4 niches x 20 keywords, weekly collection x 3 weeks, 3 engines; measured linked citations and unlinked mentions; segmented by domain authority and content format. Weekly cadence conflates temporal drift with sampling noise (no same-day reruns).
papers.relevance: Week-scale brand-presence churn of ~50% frames the WHICH-brands outcome: even in English-only, half of mentioned brands are unstable over weeks, and volatility differs sharply by vertical, which matters since the study spans two verticals (skincare vs fashion) and should report them separately. Its confound (weekly cadence mixes drift and noise) is precisely what the study's same-window 5-rep design fixes, a contrast worth stating in the write-up.

lenses.lens_summary:
The academic literature is unambiguous that a single LLM run is a sample from a distribution, not a measurement. Even under nominally deterministic settings (temperature 0, fixed seed), outputs vary across identical calls: Atil et al. (arXiv:2408.04667) found accuracy swings up to 15% across 10 reruns of the same task on production APIs, Blackwell et al. (arXiv:2410.03492) showed determinism cannot be assumed and proposed cheap uncertainty quantification from repeated runs, and Pinhanez et al. (arXiv:2509.09705) found that even on multiple-choice questions only 50-80% of items get the same answer across 10 trials from smaller models. The self-consistency line of work (Wang et al., ICLR 2023) established the standard remedy: aggregate over several samples per prompt, with most of the benefit arriving in the first handful. Consumer web UIs (ChatGPT, Gemini) run at unknown nonzero temperature with retrieval in the loop, so the study's surfaces sit at the high-variance end of everything measured in this literature.

For the study's specific outcomes, the recommendation-focused work gives concrete null baselines. Unusual.ai's rerun-stability paper (arXiv:2605.27440) is the key precedent: identical commercial buying prompts rerun the same day (N=30) overlap at only Jaccard 0.50-0.61 on recommended-brand sets, and any prompt manipulation must be judged against that floor — their paraphrases landed 21-48 points below it, showing prompt surface form (which is what an EN/Hinglish swap changes) can move recommendations far more than rerun noise. Żatuchin's category-ownership audit (arXiv:2606.23057) provides direct precedent for exactly 5 repetitions per query-model cell across the same three engine families, aggregating brand mentions over reps; it also found engines agree on the top brand in only 41.6% of queries, so engine identity will likely dwarf language as a variance source. Citations are far noisier than brands: SE Ranking measured just 9.2% three-way exact-URL overlap across three same-day runs of Google AI Mode, Profound measured 40-60% cited-domain drift over one month across ~80k prompts per engine (Perplexity most stable at 40.5%), and Advanced Web Ranking found only 49% of brands held visibility across three weekly checks.

The defensible design posture that falls out of this: 5 reps per cell is at the low end of academic practice (10 is more common) but has a direct published precedent in brand-recommendation auditing and is adequate if the analysis aggregates correctly — compute within-language, within-engine rerun overlap (Jaccard on brand sets, appearance-rate per brand) as the explicit null baseline, run all reps in a tight time window so temporal drift cannot impersonate a language effect, bootstrap confidence intervals over reps and prompts rather than reporting point estimates, and only claim an EN-vs-Hinglish effect where cross-language divergence exceeds within-language rerun divergence. Expect brand-set overlap around 0.5-0.6 within a cell, near-total URL-level citation churn (forcing domain-level, union-over-reps citation analysis), and per-engine baselines reported separately, with skincare and fashion split since vertical strongly modulates volatility.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Consistency of Factual Knowledge in Multilingual Language Models
papers.authors: Jirui Qi, Raquel Fernández, Arianna Bisazza
papers.key_findings: Introduces the RankC metric to measure whether a model ranks candidate facts the same way across languages, independent of accuracy. Multilingual models store substantially different factual knowledge per language; scaling model size improves per-language accuracy but does NOT improve cross-lingual consistency. Knowledge edits inserted in English transfer only to languages with high RankC overlap with English.
papers.methodology_notes: Probing over the BMLAMA balanced multilingual fact benchmark across multiple multilingual PLMs; consistency measured pairwise between languages with RankC; model-editing follow-up experiment. Code and data public on GitHub.
papers.relevance: Direct theoretical grounding for the core hypothesis: if parametric knowledge itself is language-inconsistent, the brand set surfaced for a Hinglish prompt can legitimately differ from its English twin even before retrieval enters. Justifies treating EN-vs-Hinglish brand-set overlap as the primary outcome, and predicts Hinglish (low-resource, romanized) should show lower consistency with English than high-resource pairs.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.authors: Chris Wendler, Veniamin Veselovsky, Giovanni Monea, Robert West
papers.key_findings: Using a logit lens on Llama-2, shows middle-layer representations of non-English prompts decode preferentially to the ENGLISH version of the semantically correct next token before shifting to the input language in final layers. The abstract 'concept space' sits closer to English than to other languages, implying English-centric bias in what the model retrieves conceptually.
papers.methodology_notes: Carefully constructed non-English prompts with unique correct single-token continuations; intermediate-embedding trajectory analysis across layers of the Llama-2 family. Code public (epfl-dlab/llm-latent-language). arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10588
papers.relevance: The mechanistic 'why' behind any observed convergence: if models pivot through English internally, English and Hinglish prompts may retrieve overlapping brand concepts, so the study should expect partial (not total) divergence. Gives the study a citable mechanism when explaining whichever direction the results go.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.authors: Lisa Schut, Yarin Gal, Sebastian Farquhar
papers.key_findings: Extends the latent-English finding to decision-making: LLMs make key lexical/semantic decisions in a representation space closest to English regardless of input/output language, emitting English-like representations for semantically loaded words (exactly the category brand names fall into) before translating out. Steering vectors computed in English work better than ones computed in the prompt language.
papers.methodology_notes: Logit-lens analysis over French, German, Dutch, Mandarin sentences plus activation-steering experiments; open-weight models. Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed at time of review.
papers.relevance: Strengthens the prior that semantically loaded choices (which brand to recommend) are computed in an English-shaped space, predicting brand overlap between EN and Hinglish variants may be higher than surface-language differences suggest, while answer phrasing/language still diverges. Useful for framing the null hypothesis.

papers.title: Faux Polyglot: A Study on Information Disparity in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.authors: Nikhil Sharma, Kenton Murray, Ziang Xiao
papers.key_findings: In RAG settings, LLMs systematically prefer documents in the same language as the query, for both retrieval and generation, and for both factual and opinion queries. When query-language documents are scarce, they fall back to high-resource (English) sources, creating 'information cocoons' and reinforcing dominant-language views.
papers.methodology_notes: Controlled RAG simulation with parallel multilingual document sets and factual + opinion queries; ACL Anthology version: https://aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-long.411/. Abstract does not disclose full language/query counts; treat effect sizes from full paper before citing numbers.
papers.relevance: The single most on-point academic prediction for the citation-source outcome: Hinglish prompts (romanized, low-resource) should trigger the fallback path to English sources, so cited domains for EN and Hinglish prompts may converge on English-language sites while Hindi-language publishers stay invisible. Motivates coding cited sources by language and country.

papers.title: Retrieval-augmented generation in multilingual settings
papers.authors: Nadezhda Chirkova, David Rau, Hervé Déjean, Thibault Formal, Stéphane Clinchant, Vassilina Nikoulina
papers.key_findings: Builds mRAG across 13 languages (queries and datastores). Off-the-shelf multilingual retrievers and generators are not enough: task-specific prompt engineering is required just to get the model to ANSWER in the user's language, and citation incorporation is much more variable for lower-resource languages.
papers.methodology_notes: 13-language mRAG pipeline study; component-wise evaluation of retriever, reranker, generator; ACL Anthology PDF: https://aclanthology.org/2024.knowllm-1.15.pdf
papers.relevance: Direct support for measuring answer language as a first-class outcome variable, not an afterthought: even well-built pipelines drift back to English. Also predicts higher run-to-run variance in citations for the Hinglish arm, which the 5-repetition design can quantify against the EN arm.

papers.title: Investigating Language Preference of Multilingual RAG Systems
papers.authors: Jeonghyun Park, Hwanhee Lee
papers.key_findings: Decomposes language preference by pipeline stage: retrievers prefer high-resource languages and the query language; generators prefer the query language or Latin-script documents, producing inconsistent outputs when multilingual evidence conflicts. Proposes DKM-RAG (translated-passage fusion) as mitigation.
papers.methodology_notes: Systematic stage-wise experiments on mRAG; ACL Anthology: https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.295/. Abstract omits exact model/language counts; full paper needed for effect sizes.
papers.relevance: The Latin-script generator preference is a distinctive wrinkle for Hinglish, which is Hindi in Latin script: it predicts Hinglish queries may behave more like English queries (pulling Latin-script/English sources) than like Devanagari Hindi would. This is a concrete, citable reason the study's Hinglish-not-Devanagari design choice matters and should be discussed.

papers.title: Linguistic Nepotism: Trading-off Quality for Language Preference in Multilingual RAG
papers.authors: Dayeon Ki, Marine Carpuat, Paul McNamee, Daniel Khashabi, Eugene Yang, Dawn Lawrie, Kevin Duh
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (abstract page notes ICML 2026 spotlight)
papers.key_findings: With document relevance held constant via controlled mixtures and model-internals measurement, models preferentially cite English sources when queried in English; the bias amplifies for lower-resource query languages and mid-context documents. Models sometimes sacrifice document relevance to satisfy language preference, i.e., citation is not purely informativeness-driven.
papers.methodology_notes: Six open-weight models, eight languages, controlled same-relevance document mixtures; citation attribution measured via model internals rather than surface citation strings alone.
papers.relevance: Establishes that WHICH sources get cited is causally sensitive to query language even when the evidence pool is fixed, which is exactly the study's citation outcome. Supports interpreting EN-vs-Hinglish citation differences as language effects rather than pure retrieval-index differences, especially for Perplexity Sonar where retrieval is observable.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Language Confusion in LLMs
papers.authors: Kelly Marchisio, Wei-Yin Ko, Alexandre Bérard, Théo Dehaze, Sebastian Ruder
papers.key_findings: Introduces the Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB, 15 typologically diverse languages): even strong LLMs fail to consistently reply in the user's desired language; English-centric and base models are worst; confusion worsens with complex prompts and higher sampling temperature.
papers.methodology_notes: LCB combines existing and new English and multilingual prompts; line-level and word-level language-fidelity metrics; multiple open and commercial models. Benchmark public (Cohere-Labs-Community/language-confusion). arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.20052
papers.relevance: The canonical citation for the study's third outcome (what language the answer comes back in) and for expecting non-trivial variance in reply language for Hinglish prompts specifically. Its temperature finding also supports logging/controlling sampling settings and treating web-UI capture (unknown temperature) as a documented limitation.

papers.title: Multilingual Large Language Models Are Not (Yet) Code-Switchers
papers.authors: Ruochen Zhang, Samuel Cahyawijaya, Jan Christian Blaise Cruz, Genta Indra Winata, Alham Fikri Aji
papers.key_findings: Benchmarks multilingual LLMs on code-switched text (including Hindi-English) across sentiment analysis, MT, summarization, and word-level language ID: zero/few-shot LLMs underperform much smaller fine-tuned models. Multilingual competence does not imply code-switching competence.
papers.methodology_notes: Four CSW tasks over established code-switching corpora; zero-shot and few-shot prompting across multiple LLM families vs fine-tuned baselines. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14235
papers.relevance: Grounds the expectation that Hinglish prompts are genuinely harder inputs, not just translated inputs, so EN-vs-Hinglish differences may reflect comprehension degradation as well as retrieval routing. Motivates the semantic-equivalence check on prompt pairs and possibly a manipulation check that the model understood the Hinglish intent.

papers.title: COMI-LINGUA: Expert Annotated Large-Scale Dataset for Multitask NLP in Hindi-English Code-Mixing
papers.authors: Rajvee Sheth, Himanshu Beniwal, Mayank Singh
papers.key_findings: Largest expert-annotated Hinglish resource: 125K+ instances, 376K+ annotations, Fleiss' kappa >= 0.81, across matrix-language ID, token-level language ID, POS, NER, and MT. Closed-source LLMs beat traditional tools and open models zero-shot on Hinglish; one-shot prompting helps consistently.
papers.methodology_notes: Three bilingual expert annotators per instance; zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning evaluations (fine-tuned NER up to 95.25 F1). Dataset on Hugging Face.
papers.relevance: Current state-of-the-art evidence that frontier closed models (the ones in the study: ChatGPT, Gemini) handle Hinglish reasonably well, so comprehension failure alone cannot be assumed to explain divergent recommendations. Also a practical resource for validating the Hinglish prompt set (romanization conventions, matrix-language balance).

papers.title: Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines
papers.authors: Nelson F. Liu, Tianyi Zhang, Percy Liang
papers.key_findings: Human audit of four generative search engines (Bing Chat, NeevaAI, perplexity.ai, YouChat): only 51.5% of generated sentences are fully supported by their citations and only 74.5% of citations actually support the sentence they attach to, despite fluent, authoritative-sounding output.
papers.methodology_notes: Human evaluation over a diverse query set with per-sentence citation-support judgments; the methodological template for auditing citation behavior of live AI search products. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09848
papers.relevance: Methodological precedent for auditing live web-UI AI search products rather than APIs, and a caution for the citation outcome: a cited domain is not necessarily the evidential source of a brand mention. Suggests the study report citation lists as 'displayed sources' rather than verified provenance.

papers.title: GEO: Generative Engine Optimization
papers.authors: Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, Tanmay Rajpurohit, Ashwin Kalyan, Karthik Narasimhan, Ameet Deshpande
papers.key_findings: Defines visibility metrics for sources inside generated answers (position-adjusted word count, subjective impression) and shows content-side interventions (statistics, quotations, citations) shift a source's visibility in generative-engine answers by up to ~40% on GEO-bench (~10K queries); keyword stuffing does not help.
papers.methodology_notes: GEO-bench: ~10K queries aggregated from nine datasets; controlled content perturbations of candidate sources; visibility deltas measured in generated answers.
papers.relevance: Supplies the citable visibility-metric vocabulary (impression/visibility share rather than rank) the study should adopt for brand and citation measurement, and establishes that citation selection is manipulable, i.e., a moving target: results should be timestamped and versioned per engine.

papers.title: ChatGPT searches in English, even when you don't
papers.authors: Tomek Rudzki (Peec AI)
papers.venue: Peec AI blog (industry study, disclosed data scale)
papers.key_findings: Analysis of 10M+ real ChatGPT prompts and 20M query fan-outs: 43% of background search queries for non-English prompts are executed in English; at least 78% of non-English sessions include English-language research (Turkish 94%, Spanish 66%). Concrete brand consequences documented: local market leaders (e.g., Allegro.pl in Poland) buried or absent in native-language sessions.
papers.methodology_notes: Observational analysis of fan-out queries with user location matched to query language (German, Polish, Spanish, Turkish, French); published 2026-02-12; vendor-published, not peer-reviewed, underlying data not public. No Hindi/Hinglish in the language set.
papers.relevance: The closest existing industry result to the study's mechanism: if ChatGPT fans out to English searches regardless of prompt language, EN and Hinglish prompts may converge on English-language citations, and Indian-language publishers lose visibility. The study extends this to Hinglish and to Gemini/Perplexity, and can cite Peec's fan-out numbers as the mechanism hypothesis. Also validates the commercial framing for Depra-style India positioning.

papers.title: New Research: AIs are highly inconsistent when recommending brands or products
papers.authors: Rand Fishkin (SparkToro) with Patrick O'Donnell (Gumshoe.ai)
papers.venue: SparkToro blog (industry study; covered by Search Engine Journal)
papers.key_findings: 600 volunteers ran 12 recommendation prompts 2,961 times across ChatGPT, Claude, and Google AI (Nov-Dec 2025): the same brand LIST recurred in <1% of repeated identical prompts and identical ordering in <0.1%. However, per-brand visibility RATE was stable: top brands in tight categories appeared in 55-77% of runs. Conclusion: rank in AI answers is noise; appearance frequency is the trackable signal.
papers.methodology_notes: Volunteer-run prompts on real (logged-in, heterogeneous) accounts, responses normalized into ordered brand lists and compared for overlap/order; not peer-reviewed; authors disclose Gumshoe conflict of interest. SparkToro page returned 403 to automated fetch; figures verified via Search Engine Journal coverage: https://www.searchenginejournal.com/ai-recommendations-change-with-nearly-every-query-sparktoro/566242/
papers.relevance: The critical null-baseline source: with 5 repetitions per cell, exact-list matching will show near-zero consistency even WITHIN a language, so the study must compare EN-vs-Hinglish differences against within-language rerun variance (as designed) and use brand presence/visibility rates aggregated across the 5 prompts per vertical, not per-run lists or ranks. Also suggests 5 reps is thin for per-prompt claims; pooling across prompts is essential.

lenses.lens_summary:
The academic record gives strong, convergent grounds to expect that query language changes all three of the study's outcomes, but through two distinct mechanisms that the study should keep separate. First, the parametric-knowledge mechanism: multilingual models do not store the same facts across languages, and consistency does not improve with scale (Qi et al., EMNLP 2023), yet the interpretability line of work (Wendler et al., ACL 2024; Schut et al., 2025) shows models route semantically loaded decisions through an English-shaped concept space regardless of prompt language. Together these predict partial convergence: brand SETS for English and Hinglish twins should overlap more than naive "different language, different knowledge" reasoning implies, with residual divergence concentrated in locally-known Indian brands that are weakly represented in English training text. Because Hinglish is Latin-script Hindi, Park and Lee's finding that generators prefer query-language or Latin-script evidence suggests Hinglish prompts may behave more like English than Devanagari Hindi would, which is a citable rationale for the study's Hinglish-first design and a caveat on generalizing results to Hindi-script users.

Second, the retrieval-and-citation mechanism, which applies directly to Perplexity Sonar and to ChatGPT/Gemini in web-search mode: query language causally shapes which documents are retrieved and cited even when relevance is held constant. Faux Polyglot (NAACL 2025) shows same-language preference with fallback to English when query-language documents are scarce; Linguistic Nepotism (2025) shows models trade citation relevance for language preference, worse for low-resource languages; Chirkova et al. (2024) show citation behavior is far more variable in lower-resource languages; and Peec AI's 10M-prompt industry analysis shows ChatGPT executes 43% of its background fan-out searches in English for non-English prompts, with at least 78% of non-English sessions touching English sources. The concrete prediction for the study: Hinglish prompts will largely surface English-language citations anyway (convergence at the source level), Indian-language publishers will be near-invisible in both arms, and any citation-language differences will be smaller than the fan-out mechanism alone would suggest. Answer language is itself an unstable outcome worth measuring: the Language Confusion Benchmark (EMNLP 2024) shows even strong models fail to reliably reply in the user's language, and the code-switching literature (Zhang et al., EMNLP 2023; COMI-LINGUA, 2025) shows Hinglish is a genuinely harder input class, though frontier closed models now handle it credibly, so comprehension failure cannot be assumed as the explanation for divergence.

On measurement, the literature is blunt about what a 10-prompt, 5-repetition design can and cannot claim. SparkToro/Gumshoe's 2,961-run study found identical brand lists recur in under 1% of reruns of the SAME prompt, while per-brand appearance rates were stable (55-77% for category leaders), and the LLM-nondeterminism literature confirms outputs vary even at temperature 0. The design's rerun-variance-as-null-baseline is therefore the right instinct, but with n=5 per cell the study should report brand presence/visibility rates pooled across the 5 prompts per vertical (GEO's position-adjusted visibility metrics are the standard vocabulary), test EN-vs-Hinglish differences against within-language rerun variance, and avoid any per-run or rank-based claims. Liu et al.'s verifiability audit (only 74.5% of citations in generative search engines actually support their sentence) argues for reporting cited domains as displayed sources rather than verified provenance. No prior study was found that measures EN-vs-Hinglish effects on brand recommendations in consumer AI search; the closest work covers European languages (Peec) or monolingual low-resource queries (academic mRAG), so the proposed study occupies a real gap, and I found no existing Hinglish AI-search study to either build on or contradict.

A decade of code-mixed NLP research established that Hinglish, which in real usage is overwhelmingly romanized rather than Devanagari, is a distinct register that standard multilingual models handle poorly. The foundational benchmarks (GLUECoS at ACL 2020, LinCE at LREC 2020) built evaluation infrastructure over romanized Hindi-English social media text and showed that multilingual pretrained models degrade on code-switched input, especially on semantic tasks like NLI and QA, unless explicitly adapted with code-switched data. The generation-side work (HinGE, HinglishEval at INLG 2022) added a second caution directly relevant to prompt construction: for any given English-Hindi sentence pair there are many acceptable Hinglish renderings, human annotators disagree substantially about their quality, and automatic systems struggle to predict those ratings. This means the "semantically equivalent EN/Hinglish pair" in the study design is a nontrivial artifact that should be validated (e.g., by bilingual review and by controlling code-mixing density with a metric like CMI), not assumed.

The LLM-era evidence is remarkably consistent about the direction of the effect: code-mixed and romanized input is harder for current models than English. Zhang et al. (EMNLP 2023) showed multilingual LLMs under zero/few-shot prompting underperform much smaller fine-tuned models on code-switched tasks; CodeMixBench (EMNLP 2025) found consistent underperformance across 18 languages; Indi-RomCoM (2026) found near-universal accuracy drops on romanized code-mixed instructions that grow monotonically with code-mixing density (e.g., roughly 7-8 points at 75% mixing even for frontier and Indic-specialized models, with small models losing up to about 17 points); and Script Gap (2025) measured up to 24-point drops on romanized vs native-script messages in a real-world Indian health triage deployment. Crucially, neither model scale nor Indic-focused pretraining closes the gap. At the same time, romanization is not uniformly harmful: RomanSetu (ACL 2024) showed romanized text can match or beat native script as an LLM interface once models are adapted, because romanized Hindi shares tokens with English and aligns more closely with English embeddings. So for consumer assistants the net effect of a Hinglish prompt on answer quality, brand selection, and retrieval behavior is genuinely uncertain, which is exactly what the study measures. The Cohere language confusion work (EMNLP 2024) separately established that even the strongest models fail to consistently reply in the language of the prompt, and that confusion worsens with complex prompts and higher sampling temperature, which both motivates the "what language does the answer come back in" outcome variable and justifies using rerun variance as the null baseline.

The gap this study fills is real: nothing in this literature measures commercially consequential outputs (which brands get recommended, which sources get cited) under code-mixed prompts. Existing work measures classification accuracy, translation quality, or instruction-following scores; the closest analogues are Indi-RomCoM's instruction tasks and Script Gap's triage decisions, both of which show that romanized code-mixed input changes model behavior, not just fluency. Three design implications follow. First, write the Hinglish prompts as romanized code-mix at a realistic, roughly constant mixing density, since degradation scales with density and romanized text is the empirically hardest and most ecologically valid condition (no Devanagari, matching real Indian user behavior and the project's own Hinglish-first decision). Second, 5 repetitions per cell is a defensible minimum given documented output instability, but report per-cell dispersion (brand-set overlap across reruns) before attributing any EN-vs-Hinglish difference to language, since temperature-driven variance is a known confound. Third, expect asymmetric effects by task type: the literature predicts Hinglish prompts may shift retrieval and citation behavior (Perplexity/Gemini web search grounding) more than raw comprehension, since comprehension of light code-mix is largely intact in frontier models while generation and retrieval behaviors are where language effects surface.

papers.title: GLUECoS: An Evaluation Benchmark for Code-Switched NLP
papers.authors: Simran Khanuja, Sandipan Dandapat, Anirudh Srinivasan, Sunayana Sitaram, Monojit Choudhury
papers.key_findings: First broad benchmark for code-switched NLP: 11 datasets spanning 6 tasks (LID, POS, NER, sentiment, QA, and a new code-switched NLI task) in English-Hindi and English-Spanish, with the Hindi-English data largely romanized social-media text. Multilingual models (mBERT-class) beat cross-lingual ones, but performance drops on semantic tasks; fine-tuning on artificially generated code-switched data gives the best results in most tasks, showing generic multilingual pretraining does not transfer cleanly to code-mix. Companion site and scripts at https://microsoft.github.io/GLUECoS/ and arXiv:2004.12376.
papers.methodology_notes: Standard per-task metrics (F1/accuracy) over 11 public datasets; released preprocessing and evaluation scripts for reproducibility; no LLM-era models (pre-GPT-3 evaluation).
papers.relevance: Establishes that romanized Hindi-English is the canonical form of Hinglish in NLP evaluation and that models systematically find it harder than monolingual input, especially on meaning-level tasks. Grounds the study's choice of romanized (no Devanagari) Hinglish prompts and predicts language-conditional behavior differences are plausible, not exotic.

papers.title: LinCE: A Centralized Benchmark for Linguistic Code-switching Evaluation
papers.authors: Gustavo Aguilar, Sudipta Kar, Thamar Solorio
papers.key_findings: Combines 10 corpora across 4 code-switched language pairs including Hindi-English (romanized) and 4 tasks (LID, NER, POS, sentiment), with a live leaderboard. Baselines (LSTM, ELMo, multilingual BERT) show code-switching remains hard and methods do not generalize across language pairs. Also at arXiv:2005.04322 and https://huggingface.co/datasets/lince.
papers.methodology_notes: Centralized leaderboard with held-out test sets to prevent overfitting; per-task standard metrics; baseline comparison across LSTM/ELMo/mBERT.
papers.relevance: Second pillar (with GLUECoS) demonstrating standardized, romanized Hindi-English evaluation is an established scientific practice; useful to cite when defending the study's EN/Hinglish pairing as building on a known evaluation paradigm rather than an ad hoc trick.

papers.title: HinGE: A Dataset for Generation and Evaluation of Code-Mixed Hinglish Text
papers.authors: Vivek Srivastava, Mayank Singh
papers.key_findings: 1,976 English-Hindi sentence pairs with 6,694 human-generated Hinglish renderings (at least two per pair) plus 2,766 synthetic Hinglish sentences from two rule-based algorithms (WAC, PAC), each quality-rated by two human annotators. Shows there are many valid Hinglish realizations of the same meaning and that synthetic code-mix is often rated poorly by humans. Also at arXiv:2107.03760.
papers.methodology_notes: Two annotators per synthetic sentence rating quality; multiple human references per source pair; dataset released for generation and evaluation research.
papers.relevance: Directly informs construction of the 10 semantically-equivalent EN/Hinglish prompt pairs: multiple Hinglish renderings exist per English prompt, so the study should document how each pair was written and ideally have a bilingual speaker verify naturalness, since an unnatural Hinglish prompt is a confound for any brand-shift finding.

papers.title: HinglishEval Generation Challenge on Quality Estimation of Synthetic Code-Mixed Text: Overview and Results
papers.authors: Vivek Srivastava, Mayank Singh
papers.key_findings: Shared task on predicting human quality ratings (1-10 scale) and annotator disagreement (0-9 scale) for synthetic Hinglish built on HinGE; 23 teams from 18 institutions registered. Systems found quality prediction hard, and annotator disagreement itself was a prediction target, confirming that what counts as good Hinglish is contested even among humans. Task site: https://sites.google.com/view/hinglisheval.
papers.methodology_notes: Two subtasks (quality rating prediction, disagreement prediction); human-annotated gold labels from two annotators; leaderboard-style comparison of 23 teams.
papers.relevance: Warns that Hinglish quality is subjective: the study should not treat its Hinglish prompts as uniquely correct translations. Publishing the exact prompt pairs (as the study plans) is the right transparency move, and citing HinglishEval preempts reviewer objections about prompt equivalence.

papers.title: Multilingual Large Language Models Are Not (Yet) Code-Switchers
papers.authors: Ruochen Zhang, Samuel Cahyawijaya, Jan Christian Blaise Cruz, Genta Indra Winata, Alham Fikri Aji
papers.key_findings: First comprehensive LLM-era audit of code-switching: benchmarks a range of multilingual LLMs under zero- and few-shot prompting across sentiment analysis, machine translation, summarization, and word-level LID on code-switched data (including Hindi-English). LLMs show promise on some tasks but significantly underperform fine-tuned models of much smaller scale; the authors conclude multilingualism does not imply code-switching proficiency. Also at arXiv:2305.14235.
papers.methodology_notes: Zero/few-shot prompting protocol compared against fine-tuned baselines across four task families; established code-switching corpora (LinCE-family datasets) as test beds.
papers.relevance: The key citation for the study's core hypothesis: even strong multilingual LLMs behave differently on code-switched input than their monolingual performance suggests, so expecting Hinglish buying prompts to elicit different behavior from ChatGPT/Gemini/Perplexity than English prompts is well-grounded.

papers.title: MEGA: Multilingual Evaluation of Generative AI
papers.authors: Kabir Ahuja, Harshita Diddee, Rishav Hada, Millicent Ochieng, Krithika Ramesh, et al. (Microsoft)
papers.key_findings: First large benchmarking of generative LLMs (GPT-4, ChatGPT vs prior SOTA) on 16 NLP datasets across 70 typologically diverse languages, including Indic languages. Generative models lag SOTA on low-resource and non-Latin-script languages, with tokenization identified as a major factor. Also at arXiv:2303.12528; code at https://github.com/microsoft/Multilingual-Evaluation-of-Generative-AI-MEGA.
papers.methodology_notes: 16 datasets, 70 languages; standardized prompting strategies (monolingual, translate-test, cross-lingual); comparison against fine-tuned SOTA per dataset.
papers.relevance: Provides the broader baseline that GPT-family models are measurably weaker in Indic languages than English, motivating why an India-geolocated, Hindi-adjacent prompt study of consumer assistants is worth running at all; also a methodological reference for disclosing prompting templates.

papers.title: RomanSetu: Efficiently unlocking multilingual capabilities of Large Language Models via Romanization
papers.authors: Jaavid Aktar Husain, Raj Dabre, Aswanth Kumar, Jay Gala, Thanmay Jayakumar, Ratish Puduppully, Anoop Kunchukuttan
papers.key_findings: Using romanized text as the interface to an English-centric LLM (Llama 2 continually pretrained and instruction-tuned on romanized data) reduces token fertility 2x-4x versus native script and matches or outperforms native-script representation across NLU, NLG, and MT tasks; romanized-text embeddings align more closely with English translations than native-script embeddings do. Also at arXiv:2401.14280.
papers.methodology_notes: Continual pretraining plus instruction tuning on romanized Indic text; evaluation across NLU/NLG/MT suites; token-fertility and embedding-alignment analyses. Companion interpretability work: RomanLens, arXiv:2502.07424.
papers.relevance: The counterweight finding: romanized Hindi is not inherently the degraded condition; for adapted models it can be the more efficient interface because it shares tokens with English. This means the study's EN-vs-Hinglish deltas could go either direction per engine, and per-engine differences (e.g., Gemini vs Perplexity Sonar) are themselves an interesting result rather than noise.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Language Confusion in LLMs
papers.authors: Kelly Marchisio, Wei-Yin Ko, Alexandre Berard, Theo Dehaze, Sebastian Ruder (Cohere)
papers.key_findings: Introduces the Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB) over 15 typologically diverse languages (Hindi included, with a noted caveat that hi/ru were not run for the monolingual Okapi subset) measuring whether models reply in the user's desired language, at line level and word level. Llama Instruct and Mistral models show high confusion; even the strongest models fail to consistently respond in the correct language; confusion worsens with complex prompts and higher sampling temperature; few-shot prompting, multilingual SFT, and preference tuning partially mitigate. Code: https://github.com/for-ai/language-confusion.
papers.methodology_notes: Line-level and word-level pass-rate metrics over monolingual and cross-lingual generation settings; existing plus newly created English and multilingual prompt sets; multiple model families compared.
papers.relevance: The direct methodological precedent for the study's third outcome variable (what language the answer comes back in). Predicts Hinglish prompts will produce mixed or inconsistent answer languages, that this varies by model family, and that temperature-driven instability is real, which justifies the 5-repetition rerun-variance null baseline.

papers.title: COMI-LINGUA: Expert Annotated Large-Scale Dataset for Multitask NLP in Hindi-English Code-Mixing
papers.authors: Rajvee Sheth, Himanshu Beniwal, Mayank Singh
papers.key_findings: Largest expert-annotated Hinglish resource to date: 125K+ instances and 376K+ annotations by three bilingual annotators (Fleiss kappa >= 0.81) covering matrix LID, token LID, POS, NER, and MT in both Devanagari and Roman scripts. Closed-source LLMs significantly outperform traditional tools and open-source models zero-shot (e.g., up to 95.25 F1 on NER, 98.77 F1 on matrix LID); one-shot prompting consistently boosts performance.
papers.methodology_notes: Three annotators per instance; Fleiss kappa reported per task; zero-shot, one-shot, and fine-tuning evaluation regimes; dataset on Hugging Face.
papers.relevance: Shows current frontier LLMs comprehend Hinglish quite well at the token/analysis level, sharpening the study's framing: any EN-vs-Hinglish brand or citation shift is unlikely to be raw comprehension failure and more plausibly reflects retrieval, grounding, or response-policy differences, which is exactly what an AEO/GEO study should claim.

papers.title: CodeMixBench: Evaluating Code-Mixing Capabilities of LLMs Across 18 Languages
papers.authors: Yilun Yang, Yekun Chai
papers.key_findings: Benchmark of 8 tasks (3 LLM-specific, 5 traditional NLP) across 18 languages from 7 language families, built with a synthetic generation pipeline combining word substitution and GPT-4 prompting. Finds consistent LLM underperformance on code-mixed datasets, especially when mixing crosses language families; training data size, model scale, and few-shot prompting help but do not close the gap. Code and data on GitHub.
papers.methodology_notes: Synthetic code-mix generation validated against human data; cross-family vs within-family mixing comparisons; multiple model scales tested.
papers.relevance: The most current peer-reviewed evidence that code-mixed degradation persists in the ChatGPT-class model generation the study will test, and that it is not an artifact of one language pair; supports generalizing from the study's Hindi-English findings with appropriate caveats.

papers.title: Indi-RomCoM: Code-Mixed Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Romanized Indic-English Instructions
papers.authors: Avisha Das, Mihir Parmar, Mohana Ramnath, Pulkit Verma
papers.key_findings: Stress-tests LLMs on romanized code-mixed (RCM) instructions: 7 instruction-following tasks, 4 Indic languages, 3 controlled code-mixing intensity levels, across proprietary, open-weight, and Indic-focused models in zero- and few-shot settings. Nearly all models degrade on RCM input, monotonically with code-mixing density; per the paper's results, even frontier models lose roughly 7-8 accuracy points at the 75% mixing level (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6 from 68.7 to 61.2; Indic-pretrained Sarvam-30B from 64.2 to 56.1) and small models lose up to about 17.5 points; detection-style tasks degrade more than reasoning tasks.
papers.methodology_notes: Controlled mixing-density manipulation (three levels) is the key design feature; zero-shot and few-shot configurations; reports per-model performance gaps relative to English baseline. Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed; exact run counts not stated in the abstract.
papers.relevance: The closest existing design to the study: instruction-style prompts, romanized Hindi-English, controlled density, frontier models, measured English-vs-code-mix gaps. Two direct takeaways: hold Hinglish prompt mixing density roughly constant across the 10 pairs, and expect model-dependent gap sizes, which makes the three-engine comparison a genuine contribution.

papers.title: Script Gap: Evaluating LLM Triage on Indian Languages in Native vs Romanized Scripts in a Real World Setting
papers.authors: Manurag Khullar, Utkarsh Desai, Poorva Malviya, Aman Dalmia, Zheyuan Ryan Shi
papers.key_findings: On real user-generated maternal and newborn health queries in five Indian languages plus Nepali, leading LLMs perform substantially worse on romanized messages than native-script equivalents, with gaps up to 24 points across languages and models; the authors project nearly 2 million excess triage errors at their partner organization and propose uncertainty-based selective routing as mitigation.
papers.methodology_notes: Real-world deployment data rather than synthetic benchmarks; native vs romanized script as the controlled contrast; per-language and per-model gap reporting. Preprint; dataset size and run counts not in the abstract.
papers.relevance: The strongest real-world-consequences evidence that romanized Indic input changes LLM decisions, not just fluency, in a live Indian deployment. It is the best analogue for arguing that romanized Hinglish buying prompts could plausibly shift which brands get recommended, and it supports geolocating the study to India where romanized input dominates actual usage.

lenses.lens_summary:
India is now the primary growth market for exactly the three assistants this study tests. Sam Altman put ChatGPT at 100 million weekly active users in India in February 2026 (OpenAI's second-largest market; largest student base), Bain's How India Shops Online 2026 independently cites 160M+ monthly actives by December 2025, Perplexity bought nationwide distribution by giving free 12-month Pro to Bharti Airtel's 360M subscribers (July 2025), and Google has pushed Gemini hard in India with free offers and a Google-Kantar adoption study. But adoption is early and demographically skewed: Google-Kantar's 8,000-person face-to-face survey (18 cities, ages 18-44, April 2025) found only 31% had ever tried a GenAI tool. The realistic Indian AI shopper in 2026 is urban, young, bilingual, and price-sensitive, which is precisely the persona whose language choice (English vs Hinglish) the study manipulates. Capgemini's 12,000-consumer, 12-country survey (India included) found 58% of consumers had replaced traditional search with GenAI for product recommendations, up from 25% in 2023, so purchase-intent prompting of assistants is an established behavior, not a hypothetical.

The English/Hinglish contrast is grounded in strong evidence that romanized code-mix is the default register of this adopter base, not an edge case. A peer-reviewed Nature Humanities & Social Sciences Communications study of 262,578 tweets from 16,710 Delhi/Mumbai users found Hinglish rose from 42% to ~60% of posts between 2015 and 2020, with 56.3% of users preferring Hinglish by 2022. A 2026 JMIR paper shows real urban Indian users spontaneously write code-mixed Hinglish queries to LLM-based systems and that even frontier models degrade on them (GPT-5 hierarchical F1 of 0.784 on intent classification, with open-weight and Indic models worse) — direct support for the study's expectation that prompt language can shift model behavior, and for using rerun variance as the null baseline since code-mix handling is noisier. Older but foundational industry research (KPMG-Google 2017: 9 of 10 new internet users are Indian-language users, with e-commerce queries in Indian languages growing faster than English in clothing and BPC; IAMAI-Kantar 2024: 886M internet users, 55% rural, ~57% of urban users preferring Indian-language content) establishes that vernacular-register commerce is a structural feature of Indian internet growth, extended today through voice and romanized text rather than Devanagari.

On the commerce side, beauty/personal care and fashion are the right categories and the brand ground truth is well documented: Redseer and Nykaa-commissioned work sizes India's BPC market at ~$21B heading to $34B by 2028 and $40B by 2030, with online BPC scaling ~2.4x in three years and quick commerce jumping from ~2% to ~16% of online BPC; Bain puts e-retail at $65-66B GMV in 2025 with fashion the largest discretionary category and Gen Z contributing 50% of incremental orders. Two developments bear directly on interpretation of results: Bain 2026 notes conversational commerce in India is nascent but gaining traction specifically in the research/comparison phase (where this study's prompts sit), and Nykaa signed a multi-year partnership with OpenAI (June 16, 2026) putting its beauty and fashion catalogue inside ChatGPT via the Agentic Commerce Protocol — meaning ChatGPT web-UI answers to Indian skincare/fashion prompts may be structurally biased toward Nykaa inventory, which the study must log (record whether connected-app/shopping surfaces appear, and date-stamp all runs). One honest gap: no disclosed-methodology data on AI referral traffic to Indian retailers specifically was found; Adobe's rigorous AI-referral series (traffic to retail sites up 1,200% YoY by Feb 2025, later converting better than non-AI traffic) is US-only, and Indian coverage is limited to partnership announcements. That absence is itself a finding: a geolocated India study measuring which brands and sources assistants surface would be filling a genuinely empty evidence slot. Throughout, sources split cleanly: peer-reviewed (Nature HSSC, JMIR) and the NBER working paper are disclosed-methodology research; Bain, Redseer, Google-Kantar, Capgemini, IAMAI-Kantar, KPMG-Google, and Adobe are industry studies with stated methods but commercial sponsors (Bain's is produced with Flipkart, Redseer's with Nykaa — treat their category framings accordingly); the Airtel and Nykaa-OpenAI items are marketing/press content useful only for factual deal terms and dates.

papers.title: India has 100M weekly active ChatGPT users, Sam Altman says
papers.authors: TechCrunch (reporting OpenAI/Sam Altman disclosures)
papers.source_type: industry-study (news report of company-disclosed figures; not independent measurement)
papers.key_findings: As of Feb 15, 2026, India has 100M weekly active ChatGPT users out of ~800M global WAU (Oct 2025 figure), making it OpenAI's second-largest market after the US and its largest student user base. OpenAI localized pricing with a sub-$5 ChatGPT Go tier, then made it free for a year in India; New Delhi office opened Aug 2025.
papers.methodology_notes: Company-disclosed figures via Altman's Times of India op-ed ahead of the India AI Impact Summit; no independent audit. Use as scale context, not as a measured statistic.
papers.relevance: Establishes that ChatGPT web UI is the single most important AI answer surface for Indian shoppers, justifying its place in the 3-engine panel and the India geolocation. The student-heavy, Go-tier user base supports testing consumer purchase-intent prompts rather than professional queries.

papers.title: How People Use ChatGPT (NBER Working Paper 34255)
papers.authors: Aaron Chatterji, Tom Cunningham, David Deming, Zoë Hitzig, Christopher Ong, Carl Shan, Kevin Wadman
papers.venue: NBER Working Paper Series (OpenAI Economic Research + Harvard)
papers.source_type: preprint (working paper; disclosed methodology, first-party OpenAI data)
papers.key_findings: By July 2025 ChatGPT reached ~10% of the world's adult population; adoption growth in the lowest-income countries was 4x that of the highest-income countries by May 2025. Non-work usage grew from 53% to >70% of messages; Practical Guidance, Seeking Information, and Writing account for ~80% of conversations — the buckets purchase-intent prompts fall into.
