papers.methodology_notes: Privacy-preserving automated classification of large samples of consumer-plan ChatGPT messages (Nov 2022–Jul 2025); country-income growth comparisons; no India-specific message-content cut published. Also summarized at https://openai.com/index/how-people-are-using-chatgpt/.
papers.relevance: The only first-party, disclosed-methodology account of what people actually ask ChatGPT; its finding that consumer/information-seeking use dominates in fast-growing lower-income markets supports the ecological validity of running everyday buying prompts against the consumer web UI rather than the API.

papers.title: 75% of Indians desire a daily growth collaborator (Google-Kantar Gen AI in India study)
papers.authors: Google India + Kantar
papers.venue: Google India blog / Gemini Day New Delhi (Apr 25, 2025)
papers.source_type: industry-study (disclosed survey methodology; Google-sponsored, promotional framing around Gemini)
papers.key_findings: Survey of 8,000+ Indians aged 18-44 across 18 tier-1/tier-2 cities (face-to-face): 60% were unfamiliar with AI and only 31% had tried any GenAI tool as of early 2025; self-reported benefit stats among Gemini early adopters (92-93% confidence/productivity boosts) are promotional.
papers.methodology_notes: n=8,000+, 18 cities, ages 18-44, two SEC household classes, face-to-face interviews. Adoption-funnel numbers are usable; Gemini-benefit percentages are marketing claims from a self-selected user group.
papers.relevance: Anchors Gemini's India push and shows the adopter base is urban, young, and early-funnel — matching the study persona. The 31% trial figure cautions against generalizing findings to 'Indian consumers' broadly; frame results as applying to current urban AI-shopper cohorts.

papers.title: Airtel partners with Perplexity: free 12-month Perplexity Pro for all 360mn customers
papers.authors: Bharti Airtel (press release); context from TechCrunch
papers.source_type: docs (marketing/press content; factual deal terms only)
papers.key_findings: Airtel gave all 360M mobile/Wi-Fi/DTH customers a free 12-month Perplexity Pro subscription (worth ~Rs 17,000), exclusive among Indian telcos, activated via the Airtel Thanks app. TechCrunch (https://techcrunch.com/2025/07/17/perplexity-sees-india-as-a-shortcut-in-its-race-against-openai) reports Perplexity treats India as its primary user-growth lever, with app downloads surging post-deal.
papers.methodology_notes: Marketing content; no usage data disclosed (subscriptions offered, not activated users). No public data on how many of the 360M activated Pro.
papers.relevance: Justifies Perplexity's inclusion in the panel despite smaller global share: in India it has telco-scale distribution, so its brand recommendations and citations plausibly reach mass-market Hinglish-first users. Also a confound note: many Indian Perplexity users are on Pro, whereas the study tests Sonar with web search; report which tier/config was measured.

papers.title: Nykaa partners with OpenAI for conversational shopping inside ChatGPT
papers.authors: MediaNama (reporting Nykaa/OpenAI announcement)
papers.source_type: docs (news coverage of a company announcement; marketing content, factual deal terms)
papers.key_findings: Nykaa signed a multi-year agreement listing its beauty and fashion storefronts as connected apps in ChatGPT via OpenAI's Agentic Commerce Protocol: Indian users asking for skincare, wedding outfits, or fragrance get recommendations drawn from Nykaa's catalogue and are routed to Nykaa to buy. Nykaa also adopts ChatGPT Enterprise and Codex internally.
papers.methodology_notes: Announcement coverage; no performance data. Cross-confirmed by Storyboard18 and other outlets same week.
papers.relevance: Directly load-bearing for the study: ChatGPT's India web UI now has a structural tilt toward Nykaa inventory in exactly the two test categories (skincare, fashion). The protocol must log whether shopping cards/connected-app surfaces appear per run, date-stamp all captures, and treat Nykaa over-representation as potentially integration-driven rather than organic model preference.

papers.title: How India Shops Online 2026
papers.authors: Arpan Sheth, Shyam Unnikrishnan, Manan Bhasin, Punit Parekh (Bain & Company, in association with Flipkart)
papers.source_type: industry-study (disclosed sources: Flipkart data, Forrester, CRISIL, RBI, TRAI, market interviews; Flipkart is a sponsor — potential conflict)
papers.key_findings: India e-retail hit $65-66B GMV in 2025 (+19-21% YoY), heading to $170-180B by 2030. Cites India as ChatGPT's second-largest market with 160M+ MAU by Dec 2025; conversational commerce is nascent for end-to-end purchase but gaining traction in product research and comparison. The 2025 edition (https://www.bain.com/insights/how-india-shops-online-2025/) adds: Gen Z is 40-45% of e-retail shoppers and 50% of incremental orders; trend-first fashion to grow from $2-2.5B (2024) to $8-10B by 2028.
papers.methodology_notes: Annual market-sizing with named data sources and participant interviews; no confidence intervals; GMV ranges given rather than point estimates.
papers.relevance: Best available market-structure map for choosing realistic prompts and interpreting brand outputs (marketplaces Flipkart/Amazon/Meesho, fashion verticals Myntra/Ajio, Gen Z discovery patterns). Its finding that AI assistants are used at the research/comparison stage validates the study's purchase-intent prompt framing as the commercially meaningful surface.

papers.title: India's $40Bn Beauty & Personal Care market: growth, shifts and opportunities for 2030 (with Nykaa-Redseer 'Beauty and the Nation' 2024 figures)
papers.authors: Redseer Strategy Consultants (portions commissioned by/with Nykaa)
papers.source_type: industry-study (consultant market sizing; Nykaa-commissioned components are marketing-adjacent)
papers.key_findings: India BPC to reach $40B by 2030 (4th largest globally); ~20 brands exceed INR 1,500 Cr revenue (FY26E). Companion Redseer material: online BPC scaled ~2.4x from ~Rs 21K Cr (CY22) to ~Rs 52K Cr (CY25); quick commerce grew from ~2% to ~16% of online BPC (GMV up ~22.5x CY22-CY25). The 2024 Nykaa-Redseer report (via https://www.indiaretailing.com/2024/09/05/india-beauty-personal-care-market-expected-to-reach-34-bn-by-2028-nykaa-report/) sized BPC at ~$21B going to $34B by 2028, with e-commerce the fastest channel at ~25% CAGR.
papers.methodology_notes: Redseer GMV estimation methodology not fully public; figures are consultant estimates, and Nykaa co-branding means channel narratives favor online/omnichannel. Use for category structure and player lists, not precise shares.
papers.relevance: Supplies the skincare-category ground truth for scoring brand mentions: which brands are large (legacy FMCG vs new D2C like Mamaearth/Minimalist/Plum vs Nykaa house brands) and how online-skewed the category is. Helps distinguish 'assistant recommends a genuinely leading brand' from long-tail hallucination in both EN and Hinglish arms.

papers.title: Indian Languages – Defining India's Internet
papers.authors: KPMG India + Google
papers.source_type: industry-study (disclosed survey methodology; dated but foundational)
papers.key_findings: 9 of 10 new Indian internet users are Indian-language-first; Indian-language user CAGR 18% vs 3% for English; 88% of Indian-language users respond better to vernacular ads than English; Indian-language queries were growing faster than English specifically in e-commerce categories including clothing and beauty/personal care.
papers.methodology_notes: Primary survey research across urban and rural India (methodology chapter in PDF); 2017 data, so magnitudes are stale even though the directional structure (vernacular-led growth) has since been confirmed by IAMAI-Kantar.
papers.relevance: The canonical citation for why prompt language matters commercially in India, and notably documents faster vernacular query growth in the exact study categories (clothing, BPC). Supports the hypothesis that Hinglish prompts represent a large, distinct demand pool that AI answers may serve differently.

papers.title: Internet in India 2024 (ICUBE)
papers.authors: IAMAI + Kantar
papers.source_type: industry-study (large-sample household survey; methodology disclosed in report)
papers.key_findings: 886M active internet users in 2024 (+8% YoY), crossing 900M in 2025; rural India is 55% of users; ~98% of users access Indic-language content and ~57% of urban users prefer consuming content in Indian languages; report flags Indic languages and AI as the next growth drivers.
papers.methodology_notes: Kantar ICUBE household survey across urban and rural India (large multi-state sample; exact n in report PDF). Content-language preference is self-reported consumption, not query-language telemetry.
papers.relevance: Current, disclosed-methodology baseline showing the Indian internet majority operates in Indian languages. Since assistants' Hinglish handling will meet this population as AI adoption deepens beyond the English-fluent early cohort, the study's Hinglish arm measures readiness for the mainstream Indian user, and the EN-vs-Hinglish gap can be framed as an equity/readiness metric.

papers.title: Social, economic, and demographic factors drive the emergence of Hinglish code-mixing on social media
papers.authors: (authors listed on article page)
papers.venue: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (Nature Portfolio)
papers.key_findings: Corpus of 262,578 tweets from 16,710 handles (Delhi + Mumbai, Jan 2014-Sep 2022; cricket/Bollywood/politics topics), code-mixing quantified via Code-Mixing Index (CMI >= 0.5 = Hinglish). Hinglish rose from 42% to ~60% of tweets (2015-2020) then stabilized; 56.3% of users preferred Hinglish by 2022; users transition from English to Hinglish at 78% probability vs 43% from Hindi; adoption correlates with socio-economic factors.
papers.methodology_notes: Longitudinal observational corpus study; CMI-based measurement; urban Hindi-belt sample (Delhi/Mumbai), so generalization to South India is limited — matching the study's Hinglish (not pan-Indic) scope.
papers.relevance: Peer-reviewed evidence that romanized Hinglish is the majority written register of urban Hindi-belt users online — the exact population buying skincare/fashion through AI assistants. Also justifies writing Hinglish prompts as natural mixed-script romanized text (measurable via CMI, which the study could report for its prompt pairs to prove equivalence of mixing depth).

papers.title: Understanding User Intent in Code-Mixed Sexual and Reproductive Health Queries in Urban India: Hierarchical Classification Approach Using Large Language Models
papers.authors: (authors listed on article page)
papers.key_findings: Built SRHQ-India, a dataset of real-world code-mixed Hinglish user queries, and benchmarked proprietary, multilingual open-weight, and Indic LLMs zero-shot on hierarchical intent classification. GPT-5 was best (h-F1 0.784, Exact Match 0.683, level-1 accuracy 0.886, level-2 0.771); Claude-3.5-Sonnet close behind (h-F1 0.745); open-weight and Indic models trailed. Confirms LLMs still struggle with code-mixed, culturally situated Indic queries.
papers.methodology_notes: Zero-shot evaluation with hierarchical F1/exact-match metrics on real user queries (dataset size in paper); health domain, not commerce, so transfer to shopping intents is indicative rather than direct.
papers.relevance: The closest peer-reviewed analogue to the study's core question: real Indian users do query AI systems in Hinglish, and even frontier models lose 10-25 accuracy points on such input. Predicts measurable EN-vs-Hinglish differences in interpretation quality, and supports 5 repetitions per cell since degraded comprehension plausibly raises answer variance.

papers.title: What Matters to Today's Consumer (4th edition) — 71% of consumers want generative AI integrated into their shopping experiences
papers.authors: Capgemini Research Institute
papers.source_type: industry-study (disclosed methodology: 12,000 consumers 18+, 12 countries across NA/Europe/APAC incl. India, surveyed Oct-Nov 2024)
papers.key_findings: 58% of consumers have replaced traditional search engines with GenAI tools for product/service recommendations (up from 25% in 2023); 71% want GenAI integrated into purchasing; 68% want AI to aggregate search/social/retailer results; ~75% open to GenAI recommendations. India is named among countries leading quick-delivery willingness; no public India-only cut of the AI-recommendation stats.
papers.methodology_notes: n=12,000, 12 countries, fielded Oct-Nov 2024 (methodology stated in press release, verified in PDF). Global aggregate; India in sample but country-level splits not published. Companion 2025 report 'From hype to habit' (10,000 consumers, 13 countries) adds: 53% have purchased based on GenAI recommendations.
papers.relevance: Quantifies the behavioral shift the study instruments: majority of surveyed consumers now use GenAI instead of search for product recommendations, making assistant brand selection a real commercial gatekeeper. Justifies purchase-intent prompt design mimicking recommendation-seeking ('best face wash for oily skin...') rather than navigational queries.

papers.title: Adobe Analytics: Traffic to U.S. Retail Websites from Generative AI Sources Jumps 1,200 Percent
papers.authors: Adobe Digital Insights (Vivek Pandya)
papers.source_type: industry-study (disclosed methodology; US-only — included as marked proxy because no India-specific AI-referral dataset was found)
papers.key_findings: AI-source referral traffic to US retail sites rose 1,200% between Jul 2024 and Feb 2025; AI-referred visitors showed higher engagement (longer sessions, more pages) but initially converted worse than other channels — later Adobe/press updates (e.g. https://www.digitalcommerce360.com/2026/06/17/adobe-ai-referred-traffic-to-retail-sites-doubles-in-a-year/) show conversion flipping to +42% vs non-AI traffic by 2026 and continued 100%+ YoY growth.
papers.methodology_notes: Adobe Analytics panel of 1T+ visits to US retail sites plus a companion consumer survey (~5,000 US respondents). Explicitly not India data: no equivalent disclosed-methodology AI-referral series for Indian retailers exists publicly as of Aug 2026 — Indian evidence is limited to partnership announcements (Nykaa-OpenAI) and platform claims.
papers.relevance: Documents the mechanism that gives the study stakes (AI answers now route measurable, increasingly high-converting retail traffic) while flagging the India-shaped hole in the evidence: the proposed 10-prompt study would produce some of the first public India-geolocated data on which retailers and sources AI assistants actually surface, in either language.

papers.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
papers.authors: Evan Miller (Anthropic)
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (widely cited; accompanied by Anthropic research blog post)
papers.key_findings: Treats LLM evals as experiments drawn from an unseen super-population and imports standard experimental-analysis machinery: compute standard errors of the mean via CLT, use CLUSTERED standard errors when questions are drawn in related groups, reduce variance by resampling answers per question (K repetitions), and do inference on question-level PAIRED differences when comparing two conditions. Includes explicit power-analysis formulas for deciding how many questions/resamples are needed to detect a given effect size.
papers.methodology_notes: Analytic paper with worked formulas rather than a new benchmark; the resampling recommendation (multiple completions per item, variance decomposed into between-item and within-item components) and the paired-differences-with-clustered-SE recipe map one-to-one onto a prompts-as-clusters design. Recommends reporting standard errors and CIs, never bare point scores.
papers.relevance: This is the closest thing to a canonical citation for the study's whole inferential frame. The 10 prompts are the clusters, the 5 reps are the within-item resamples, and EN-vs-Hinglish is a paired comparison at the prompt level, so inference should run on prompt-level paired differences with clustered/aggregated variance, not on the 300 raw runs as if independent. Its power formulas also let the methodology section state honestly what effect sizes 10 prompts x 5 reps can and cannot detect.

papers.title: Position: Don't Use the CLT in LLM Evals With Fewer Than a Few Hundred Datapoints
papers.authors: Sam Bowyer, Laurence Aitchison, Desi R. Ivanova
papers.key_findings: Shows empirically that CLT/Wald-style error bars dramatically underestimate uncertainty in LLM evals with fewer than a few hundred datapoints, and recommends easy-to-implement alternatives: frequentist intervals with correct small-sample coverage (Wilson-type) and Bayesian (Beta-Binomial) intervals, including treatment of paired model comparisons and clustered questions. Code released at github.com/sambowyer/no_clt_paper.
papers.methodology_notes: Coverage simulations across small-N regimes comparing Wald/CLT intervals against Wilson and Bayesian alternatives; explicit sections on paired comparisons and question clustering at small N. PMLR version: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/bowyer25a.html
papers.relevance: Directly governs this study's regime: per-cell n=5 and per-engine-per-language n=50 runs (25 per category) are exactly the 'fewer than a few hundred datapoints' setting. It is the modern, LLM-specific authority for why the study must use Wilson (or Bayesian) intervals rather than naive plus-or-minus-1.96-SE error bars, and it can be cited verbatim to justify the choice against a reviewer who asks why not t-tests.

papers.title: Interval Estimation for a Binomial Proportion
papers.authors: Lawrence D. Brown, T. Tony Cai, Anirban DasGupta
papers.key_findings: The canonical demonstration that the textbook Wald interval has chaotic, badly deficient coverage even at moderate n and p away from 0/1, and the standard recommendation of the Wilson score interval (or Jeffreys interval) for small n and Agresti-Coull for larger n.
papers.methodology_notes: Exhaustive coverage-probability analysis across n and p; DOI 10.1214/ss/1009213286. This is the reference statisticians expect to see next to any Wilson-interval claim.
papers.relevance: The primary citation for every proportion reported in the study: brand-mention rate (how often brand X appears across reps), citation-domain share, and answer-language rate per condition. With n as small as 5-50, Wald intervals would be indefensible; citing Brown/Cai/DasGupta plus Bowyer et al. makes the Wilson choice bulletproof. Also useful for the honest framing that a 3/5 per-cell rate carries a Wilson 95% CI of roughly 0.23-0.88, i.e. per-cell claims are off the table.

papers.title: Jaccard/Tanimoto Similarity Test and Estimation Methods for Biological Presence-Absence Data
papers.authors: Neo Christopher Chung, Blazej Miasojedow, Michal Startek, Anna Gambin
papers.key_findings: Provides statistical estimation and significance testing for Jaccard/Tanimoto coefficients on presence-absence (set) data: expected Jaccard under independence, centered coefficients, exact and asymptotic p-values, and a recommended BOOTSTRAP procedure for significance when exact computation is impractical. Ships as the open-source R package 'jaccard'.
papers.methodology_notes: Simulation studies show the bootstrap and measure-concentration approximations produce accurate p-values and FDR at a fraction of exact-solution cost. The key conceptual import: a raw Jaccard value is uninterpretable without a null expectation, because even independent sets share elements by chance.
papers.relevance: The study's headline metric, overlap between the brand set recommended under EN and under Hinglish, is a Jaccard statistic on small sets. This paper supplies (a) the citable case that raw Jaccard needs a null reference, and (b) bootstrap machinery for CIs/p-values. In our design the natural null is empirical rather than independence-based: within-condition rerun Jaccard (rep-to-rep overlap among the 5 same-language reruns) is the noise floor, and cross-language Jaccard is compared against that distribution, but this citation grounds the general treat-Jaccard-as-a-statistic-with-uncertainty stance.

papers.title: Permutation Methods: A Basis for Exact Inference
papers.authors: Michael D. Ernst
papers.key_findings: Accessible authoritative treatment of permutation/randomization tests: when they are exact and distribution-free, how to construct them for paired and two-sample designs, and why they are the method of choice when sample sizes are too small for asymptotic tests.
papers.methodology_notes: DOI 10.1214/088342304000000396. For a paired design with 10 units, the full sign-flip permutation distribution has 2^10 = 1024 elements, small enough to enumerate exactly, so the reported p-value is exact rather than approximate.
papers.relevance: The clean citation for the study's main hypothesis test: for each engine, compute a per-prompt statistic (e.g., cross-language brand-set Jaccard minus mean within-language rerun Jaccard, or difference in brand-mention rate) and run an exact paired sign-flip permutation test across the 10 prompts. No normality assumption, exact at N=10, and trivially explainable in a public methods section.

papers.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Testing Statistical Significance in Natural Language Processing
papers.authors: Rotem Dror, Gili Baumer, Segev Shlomov, Roi Reichart
papers.venue: ACL 2018 (Proceedings of the 56th Annual Meeting of the ACL, Long Papers, pp. 1383-1392)
papers.key_findings: The standard NLP-community protocol for significance-test selection: use nonparametric tests (sign/McNemar, Wilcoxon, paired bootstrap, permutation/randomization) when metric distributions are unknown or samples are small; matches test type to evaluation-measure type; documents that a large share of ACL/TACL papers misuse or omit significance testing.
papers.methodology_notes: Survey plus decision-protocol paper; its decision tree explicitly routes small-sample, non-normal, paired NLP comparisons to exact nonparametric tests. This is the reference NLP reviewers expect for test-choice justification.
papers.relevance: Bridges the pure-statistics citations (Ernst, Brown et al.) to NLP practice: it lets the methodology section say the paired-permutation and bootstrap choices follow the established ACL protocol for paired system comparisons, which matters for a publicly citable study likely to be read by both marketing and NLP audiences.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of the Non-determinism of ChatGPT in Code Generation
papers.authors: Shuyin Ouyang, Jie M. Zhang, Mark Harman, Meng Wang
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology; arXiv:2308.02828
papers.key_findings: Across 829 problems, identical prompts to ChatGPT yield highly unstable outputs across reruns; they quantify rerun instability with semantic, syntactic, and structural similarity measures across repeated requests, and show temperature=0 reduces but does NOT eliminate non-determinism.
papers.methodology_notes: Methodological template: fixed prompt, repeated requests, then pairwise similarity among the repetitions as the measured quantity. This 'similarity among reruns of the same condition' construct is exactly the study's null baseline, just with brand sets instead of code.
papers.relevance: Primary precedent for the study's core design decision to use rerun variance as the null: if rep-to-rep brand-set overlap within the SAME language is itself low, a low EN-vs-Hinglish overlap means nothing. Also citable for why 1 run per cell (common in AEO industry studies) is methodologically invalid, and why the study cannot assume web-UI ChatGPT is deterministic.

papers.title: Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings
papers.authors: Berk Atil, Sarp Aykent, Alexa Chittams, Lisheng Fu, Rebecca J. Passonneau, et al.
papers.key_findings: Five LLMs configured for maximum determinism, eight tasks, 10 runs each: accuracy still varied by up to 15% across runs, with best-to-worst-run gaps up to 70% on some tasks; no model delivered repeatable accuracy across all tasks, let alone identical output strings. Attributes residual non-determinism partly to batched/co-mingled inference serving, i.e. it is structural and not going away.
papers.methodology_notes: 10 repetitions per condition as the variance-measurement budget; reports spread (best/worst/across-run variance) rather than single scores. Useful as the closest published anchor for 'how many reps': they used 10; 5 is a defensible minimum if the analysis aggregates across 10 prompts, but the limitations section should acknowledge it.
papers.relevance: Strongest citation for the claim that even 'deterministic' settings do not remove run-to-run variance, so consumer web UIs (no temperature control at all) certainly will not. Directly supports the 5-repetitions-per-cell design and supports framing every per-cell number as a sample from a distribution. Also useful to preempt the objection 'why not just set temperature to 0 via API' for the Perplexity Sonar arm.

papers.title: The Good, The Bad, and The Greedy: Evaluation of LLMs Should Not Ignore Non-Determinism
papers.authors: Yifan Song, Guoyin Wang, Sujian Li, Bill Yuchen Lin
papers.venue: arXiv:2407.10457 (evaluated at NAACL-era benchmarks; code at github.com/Yifan-Song793/GoodBadGreedy)
papers.key_findings: Single-output evaluation misrepresents model behavior: across benchmarks there are consistent, sizeable gaps between greedy decoding and sampled generations, and substantial spread across sampled completions of the same prompt; alignment (RLHF/DPO) reduces but does not remove sampling variance.
papers.methodology_notes: Runs many sampled completions per item and reports the distribution (and best-of-N) rather than one draw. Reinforces that the object of measurement for a sampled system is a per-prompt DISTRIBUTION over outputs.
papers.relevance: Since ChatGPT and Gemini web UIs sample at an unknown non-zero temperature, each of the study's cells is a 5-draw sample from a distribution over brand slates. This paper is the citation for reporting per-cell results as distributions (e.g., brand appears in k-of-5 reps) instead of treating any single capture as 'the answer', and for the claim that industry one-shot AEO screenshots are not evidence.

papers.title: State of What Art? A Call for Multi-Prompt LLM Evaluation
papers.authors: Moran Mizrahi, Guy Kaplan, Dan Malkin, Rotem Dror, Dafna Shahaf, Gabriel Stanovsky
papers.key_findings: Analysis of 6.5M instances across 20 LLMs and 39 tasks shows single-prompt-template evaluation is brittle: paraphrases of the same instruction change both absolute scores and MODEL RANKINGS. Proposes evaluating over a set of prompt paraphrases and reporting distribution-aware metrics.
papers.methodology_notes: Large-scale paraphrase collection; quantifies between-template variance as often comparable to between-model differences. Implication for small studies: prompt identity is a major variance component and must be treated as a random factor, not averaged away silently.
papers.relevance: Justifies the 10-prompt (5 skincare + 5 fashion) design over any single 'best prompt', and warns the limitations section: with 10 prompts, generalization is to these prompt types, not to 'all Indian buying queries'. Also supports analyzing prompts as the unit of inference (matching Miller's clustered-SE guidance) because between-prompt variance will likely dominate between-rep variance.

papers.title: REFORMS: Consensus-based Recommendations for Machine-learning-based Science
papers.authors: Sayash Kapoor, Emily Cantrell, Kenny Peng, et al. (19-researcher consensus, Princeton-led)
papers.key_findings: A 32-item, 8-module consensus checklist for reporting ML-based science, covering study goals, data provenance and collection dates, preprocessing, metric definitions fixed before analysis, uncertainty quantification, compute/version documentation, and public release of data and code to prevent the validity/reproducibility failures common in ML-adjacent studies.
papers.methodology_notes: Consensus/Delphi-style standards paper rather than an experiment; designed exactly for studies where ML systems are the measurement instrument. The checklist is short enough to adopt wholesale as an appendix.
papers.relevance: The credibility backbone for a publicly citable industry study: following REFORMS means disclosing exact prompt texts (both languages), capture dates and times, geolocation method (IP/VPN/account region), model/UI version identifiers, the full 300-run raw dataset, brand-extraction and alias-matching rules fixed BEFORE analysis, and all code. Citing and visibly complying with REFORMS is what separates this study from typical AEO marketing content.

papers.title: Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks
papers.authors: Lovish Madaan, Aaditya K. Singh, Rylan Schaeffer, Andrew Poulton, Sanmi Koyejo, Pontus Stenetorp, Sharan Narang, Dieuwke Hupkes
papers.key_findings: Defines and empirically measures a battery of variance components in LLM benchmarks (seed variance, choice-format variance, monotonicity) across many models, showing that unquantified variance frequently swamps the performance differences papers claim, and that some intuitive variance-reduction tricks from human psychometrics fail to help.
papers.methodology_notes: Variance-decomposition framing: name each variance source, estimate it empirically, and only then interpret condition differences. The study's analogue sources are: rep-to-rep sampling noise, prompt-to-prompt variance, engine version drift over the capture window, and geolocation/session effects.
papers.relevance: Citable for the study's overall logic: before attributing brand-slate differences to prompt LANGUAGE, quantify how much slates differ under no change at all (the rerun baseline) and across prompts within a language. Also motivates compressing the capture window and recording engine/UI versions, since temporal drift is an uncontrolled variance source the paper documents in benchmark settings.

lenses.lens_summary:
The statistics literature and the newer LLM-evaluation literature converge on one message for a 10-prompt x 3-engine x 2-language x 5-rep study: the design is workable, but only if inference is done at the right unit with small-sample methods. On proportions (brand-mention rates, citation-domain shares, answer-language rates), Brown, Cai and DasGupta (2001) is the canonical demonstration that Wald/CLT intervals fail at these sample sizes, and Bowyer et al. (ICML 2025) re-proves the point specifically for LLM evals under a few hundred datapoints, recommending exactly the Wilson-or-Bayesian intervals this study plans. Practically: per-cell n=5 proportions are almost pure noise (a 3/5 rate has a Wilson 95% CI of roughly 0.23-0.88), so all confirmatory claims must aggregate, per engine, across the 10 prompts and 5 reps, with prompts treated as clusters per Miller (2024), whose super-population framing, clustered standard errors, paired-differences recipe, and power formulas give the study its complete inferential skeleton.

For the headline set-overlap question, the right pattern combines two strands. Chung et al. (2019) establishes that a Jaccard coefficient is a statistic requiring a null reference and uncertainty (they supply bootstrap significance machinery and an R package); the LLM non-determinism strand (Ouyang et al. on ChatGPT reruns; Atil et al. showing up to 15% accuracy swings across 10 runs even at 'deterministic' settings; Song et al. on sampling spread) establishes that the correct null for this study is empirical rerun variance, i.e., rep-to-rep brand-set Jaccard within the same language and engine is the noise floor against which EN-vs-Hinglish Jaccard must be compared. The cleanest confirmatory test is then an exact paired permutation test across the 10 prompts (per-prompt statistic: cross-language overlap minus within-language rerun overlap, or paired difference in brand-mention rate), which with 2^10 = 1024 sign-flips is exact and assumption-free (Ernst 2004), and follows the standard NLP protocol for paired system comparisons (Dror et al., ACL 2018). Mizrahi et al. (TACL 2024) and Madaan et al. (2024) supply the variance-decomposition caveats: prompt-template variance is typically large relative to condition effects, so the study should report per-prompt results transparently and generalize only to prompts like these, not to all Indian buying queries.

Two honest framings follow. First, power: with 10 prompts as the effective inferential unit, only large language effects (on the order of 25-40 percentage-point shifts in brand-mention rates, or overlap gaps well outside the rerun-noise band) will reach significance; the study should therefore be framed primarily as ESTIMATION with intervals (Wilson CIs on proportions, bootstrap CIs on Jaccard, per-engine effect sizes) rather than as a null-hypothesis verdict, with the permutation test as a conservative headline check. Second, reporting: the REFORMS checklist (Kapoor et al., Science Advances 2024) plus Miller's reporting recommendations define what a credible public methodology section must disclose — exact prompt pairs, capture dates/window, geolocation mechanism, model/UI versions, brand-alias extraction rules fixed before analysis, every raw run (all 300), the rerun-variance baseline alongside every condition effect, and released code. Following that checklist is what will let this study be cited as evidence rather than dismissed as AEO marketing.
